source1: N. Neela and G. Ambrosia, 'Contribution of Marathas of Tanjore to Art and Architecture', Shanlax International Journal of Arts, Science and Humanities 3(3), 2016 - https://shanlaxjournals.in/journals/index.php/sijash/article/view/1206/1023
source2: Dominik Wujastyk, 'Thanjavur Library as a Realm of Knowledge', National Mission for Manuscripts newsletter, 2006 (UCL Discovery) - https://discovery-pp.ucl.ac.uk/3276/1/3276.pdf
notes: Chokkanatha of Madurai destroyed Tanjore Nayak power in 1673; Ekoji occupied Tanjore in 1675 and founded the Maratha kingdom. All three courts were Hindu; the Marathas patronized temples, Sanskrit learning and Brahmin scholars.

source1: Banglapedia (Asiatic Society of Bangladesh), 'Chandra Dynasty, The' (after A.M. Chowdhury, Dynastic History of Bengal, 1967) - https://en.banglapedia.org/index.php/Chandra_Dynasty,_The
notes: Chandra kings were Buddhist but settled Brahmins, last two Vaishnava-leaning; population religion not stated, so database value kept. Karna's attack ended the Chandras; the Vaishnava Varmans (copperplates) took power and also patronized Buddhism.

source1: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Sogdiana iii. History and Archeology' - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/sogdiana-iii-history-and-archeology
notes: Iranica: Sogdiana was dominated by an unreformed Zoroastrianism (Nana cult); Qutayba's systematic conquest began 705, Samarkand fell 712. Britannica instead calls the region primarily Buddhist. The Umayyad Muslim rulers kept Islam; Sogdian conversion was gradual.

Coded the Medes: they took Assur and led the sack of Nineveh; Britannica says Media took Assyria with Harran (Iranica notes dispute). Median religion was a pre-Zoroastrian Mazdaism with Magi; no adoption attested; no Median archives. Babylonian partner was Mesopotamian.

Kanem-Bornu was an Islamic state from the late-11th-century conversion of its mai. Rabih, a Muslim military leader from the Sudan, sacked Kuka in 1893 and ruled from Dikwa with a highly centralized administration.

source1: National Geographic Society Education, 'Three Crowned Kings of Tamilakam' - https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/three-crowned-kings-tamilakam/
notes: The Chola rulers were mostly Hindu; they were defeated by the neighbouring Pandyas and Chola rule ended in 1279. The Pandyas had become Shaivas after earlier Jainism and controlled the southern plains as far as Nellore by 1257.

The Pratiharas were a dynasty of medieval Hindu India ruling from Kannauj. The Gahadavalas took Varanasi, Ayodhya and Kannauj under Chandradeva (c. 1089-1103); their polity depended on Brahmanical ideology and left many epigraphic records.

source2: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Harar Jugol, the Fortified Historic Town' - https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1189
notes: Harar, former capital of Muslim Adal and an independent emirate from the 17th century, called the fourth holy city of Islam, was occupied by Khedivial Egypt 1875-85. Both rulers and conquerors were Muslim; Egypt had a literate bureaucracy.

source1: Francois Vallat, 'Elam vi. Elamite religion', Encyclopaedia Iranica - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/elam-vi
source2: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Elam i. The history of Elam' - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/elam-i
notes: Coded Shimashki Elamites (took Ur 2004 BCE, Ibbi-Sin captive). At Susa Kindattu and Idadu I built Inshushinak shrines; Idadu invoked only Shamash, Ishtar, Sin; no plateau gods imposed. Akkadian cuneiform used. Coding Isin instead gives same tradition.

source2: Shaun O'Sullivan, 'Coptic Conversion and the Islamization of Egypt', Mamluk Studies Review 10(2), 2006 - https://knowledge.uchicago.edu/nanna/record/958/files/MSR_X-2_2006-OSullivan.pdf
notes: The Ismaili Fatimids, with Ismailism as state religion, conquered Egypt in 969. O'Sullivan places a Muslim majority in Egypt by the 9th-10th century, though Little and el-Leithy put decisive conversion in the 14th century.
